claims.text: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi is a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi exhibits temperature-dependent plastic deformation behavior.
Lattice distortion and microstructural heterogeneity enable multiple deformation mechanisms that respond differently to temperature.
The as-homogenized CoCrFeMnNi material is a single-phase solid solution.
As-homogenized CoCrFeMnNi has a fine-grained microstructure.
Selective-laser-melted equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi can contain fine grains, dislocation networks, and nanoscale oxides.
As-homogenized CoCrFeMnNi can contain Cr-, Mn-, and O-rich oxide particles.
The random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii produces significant lattice distortion.
The random distribution of the principal elements produces fine grains and nanoscale oxide precipitates.
Lattice distortion, fine grains, and oxide precipitates mediate dislocation dynamics and twinning.
At low temperatures, CoCrFeMnNi deformation is dominated by dislocation nucleation and propagation, potentially accompanied by stacking faults or twinning.
At elevated temperatures, thermal activation enables grain-boundary sliding, transformation-induced plasticity, and dynamic recovery in CoCrFeMnNi.
Multiple temperature-dependent mechanisms provide a favorable strength-ductility trade-off over a wide temperature range.
Yield stress decreases with increasing temperature because of thermal activation.
The alloy maintains adequate work hardening and ductility at higher temperatures.
Twinning and phase transformation compensate for thermal softening and preserve work hardening and ductility.
The proposed behavior holds only within the single-phase stability range, while phase changes or intermetallic formation can alter the mechanisms.
Yield-stress changes and the relative contributions of deformation mechanisms vary with processing route, alloy composition, and short-range ordering.

contradictions.description: The conditions and boundary require a stable single-phase material without phase decomposition, while the proposed mechanism and outcome invoke transformation-induced plasticity and phase transformations. The hypothesis does not distinguish permissible stress-induced transformations from excluded loss of phase stability.
